topic: Pollinator Decline, Species Richness, and Trophic Network Stability
scientific_summary: Agricultural intensification and landscape homogenization cause steep declines in Apoidea (wild bees), Syrphidae (hoverflies), and Lepidoptera. Loss of continuous floral resource availability creates seasonal starvation bottlenecks. Restoring polycultural flowering margins with asynchronous bloom phenology elevates wild pollinator species richness by 50-80% and increases fruit set in adjacent crops.

interventions.name: Asynchronous Phenological Floral Stepping Stones & Nesting Banks
interventions.mechanism: Planting a calibrated mix of native perennial forbs providing uninterrupted nectar and pollen across March-October, combined with untilled compacted sandy-loam bare earth banks, supports both cavity-nesting and ground-nesting solitary bee species (70% of wild bees).

quantitative_impact.crop_pollination_efficiency: +22% higher seed set in entomophilous crops

interventions.name: Rewilding Hedgerow Corridors and Deadwood Microhabitats
interventions.mechanism: Installing coarse woody debris (logs >20cm diameter) and thorny native hedgerows (e.g., Crataegus, Prunus spinosa) provides saproxylic beetle habitats, fungal sporocarp substrates, and protective predator refugia against avian raptors.

topic: Soil Macrofauna and Earthworm Density as Primary Ecological Engineers
scientific_summary: Intensive inversion tillage reduces anecic earthworm (e.g. Lumbricus terrestris) populations by 70-90% by destroying permanent vertical burrows and exposing worms to desiccation and predation. Loss of anecic worms degrades deep macropore networks, restricting water infiltration and root exploration in subsoils.

interventions.name: Conservation Minimum-Tillage with High Surface Residue Retention
interventions.mechanism: Cessation of deep inversion plowing and retention of >30% organic crop residues preserves vertical macropores, moderates topsoil temperature, and provides a continuous cellulose/lignin food supply for soil detritivores.
